newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. official challenges Israeli settlement policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official challenges Israeli settlement policy.

text.p: The U.S. consul general in Jerusalem challenged Israel's settlement policy on Tuesday, saying there was no need to expand Jewish outposts while a quarter of the homes in them stood empty.

"Based on what we've seen on the ground, the figure of 25 percent vacancy rate in settlements is more or less accurate. There's no need for natural growth of settlements if there's such a high vacancy rate," Edward Abington told Reuters.

The settlement issue has taken centre stage in a crisis in PLO-Israeli peace talks suspended since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent bulldozers to start work in March on 6,500 homes for Jews in Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem.

Netanyahu said the project at Har Homa, or Jabal Abu Ghneim as Arabs call the site, and the widening of existing settlements in the West Bank and Gaza Strip are part of "natural growth" in which housing must be provided for an expanding population.
Abington spoke three days after the PLO accused the United States of abandoning its long-held opposition to Jewish settlement construction on land Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

The U.S. diplomat also reaffirmed the 25 percent vacancy figure just hours after Netanyahu rejected the validity of a U.S. study, leaked to the left-wing Israeli Haaretz daily, that found more than a quarter of homes in settlements were empty.
"This is a groundless assertion, I can assure you this is not the situation," Netanyahu told reporters during a tour of Jewish settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday.

The U.S. State Department acknowledged it recently completed a study of Israeli settlement activity but refused to confirm a published report it found more than a quarter of settler homes were vacant.

"I can't speak specifically about this report because it has not been made public but we have from time to time and just recently tried to establish a basis of information for ourselves and for the Congress on this issue and we've done that," State Department Nicholas Burns told reporters.

A senior U.S. official told Reuters last week the Palestinians were angered by Washington's inability, during a failed peace mission by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, to persuade Israel to freeze work on the East Jerusalem project.

The U.S. official, who asked not to be identified, said the PLO also was angered by U.S. attempts to avoid a fight now with Israel over settlements. He said Washington wanted the settlement question dealt with only in future talks on a permanent peace accord.
PLO officials said the United States has abandoned its characterisation of settlements as "illegal" or "obstacles to peace."
Abington declined to say whether the adminstration of President Bill Clinton considered settlements illegal. "They're an obstacle," he said.

"Why don't we press Israel on the settlements? Settlements are one among a number of issues that Palestinians are concerned about and Israelis are concerned about, and to single out one issue and not focus on other issues doesn't really move the process forward," Abington said.
Some 130,000 Jews have settled among two million Palestinians in parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip, not counting settlement in East Jerusalem.
